nature-found-075.title: Pollutants: when a substance becomes a problem
nature-found-075.text: Oil occurs naturally, yet it can still be a pollutant. A pollutant is a substance or form of energy put into the environment that has unwanted effects or makes a resource less useful. Some occur naturally; others are made by people, such as manufactured materials and by-products. A pollutant becomes pollution, or a health concern, once its concentration is high enough to do significant harm. It can then damage plant and animal growth, human health, resources people use, or property values. Some pollutants break down naturally. Others, such as the insecticide DDT, break down into products that are themselves pollutants. Measured against the planet's safe limits, mapped in {{ref:nature-eco-597}}, people have released novel entities, new kinds of substance, well beyond safe levels. Because pollutants cross borders, international rules are needed, such as {{ref:nature-found-099}}, signed in 2004.

nature-found-079.title: Pollution: nine million deaths and an unpaid bill
nature-found-079.text: In 2019 pollution killed about nine million people, about one in six of all deaths. Roughly three-quarters of them died from air pollution. Pollution is the release into the natural environment of contaminants that cause harm. It can be any substance, solid, liquid or gas, or energy such as heat, sound, light or radioactivity. The word usually means contaminants from human sources such as manufacturing, mining, poor handling of waste, transport or farming. Pollution can come from a point source, one concentrated site such as a factory, or a nonpoint source, spread out like farm runoff. Economists treat pollution from manufacturing as a negative production externality, imposing health and clean-up costs on all of society. Goods that pollute tend to be overproduced and underpriced, because the harm is not priced into the market. Polluting industries and waste sites are often placed near vulnerable and marginalized communities, a core reason for the movement for environmental fairness explored in {{ref:nature-gov-168}}. Many sources went unregulated during industrialization, until environmental regulation emerged in the later 20th century.

nature-found-088.title: The tyranny of small decisions: how marshes vanish plot by plot
nature-found-088.text: Between 1950 and 1970, almost 50 percent of the coastal marshlands of Connecticut and Massachusetts were lost. They went through hundreds of small conversions. Ecologist William Odum pointed this out in 1982, applying an idea called the tyranny of small decisions. It describes how many small decisions, each insignificant on its own, can add up to a large outcome that nobody chose or wanted. Economist Alfred E. Kahn introduced the idea in a 1966 essay and described it as a common route to market failure. His example was the passenger railway serving Ithaca. It was withdrawn because travellers' trip-by-trip choices did not cover its costs, though many would have paid to keep it. Each choice of one option over another is also a vote to remove the other option, which may then disappear. Lakes choked by excess nutrients, land drying out into barren country and the plight of most endangered species are said to stem from series of small decisions. One remedy is to build and protect higher levels of decision-making, from local to global, though these can push decisions back down.

nature-found-092.title: An asset's own rate of return
nature-found-092.text: How much is one more unit of an asset worth tomorrow? The answer is its yield, or own rate of return: the growth expected tomorrow if one more unit is added to a portfolio today. For produced capital, yield is its {{ref:nature-econ-310}}. For a fishery or a tree, it is the growth in living material obtained by waiting. Investment can therefore be passive: restoring a wetland is investment, and so is conservation, which can simply mean waiting. Applied to {{ref:nature-found-010}}, the idea lets nature be compared with other assets. Yield is a pure number per unit of time. The UK government's long-term bonds have historically averaged about 4% a year, though more recently closer to 1%. Because relative prices change unless the economy is stationary, own rates are not enough: the rate of return on an asset is its yield plus its capital gains over a unit of time.

nature-found-095.title: Why Nature's mobility and silence breed externalities
nature-found-095.text: No one can contain the air they foul or the rivers they pollute. Externalities arise from the biosphere because {{ref:nature-econ-621}} to large parts of it are weakly defined or enforced, and because Nature is mobile, silent and invisible. An {{ref:nature-found-031}} is an unaccounted-for consequence of one person's actions for others, including future people. The harm from fouled air or water is non-excludable. Nitrogen and phosphorus where a river meets the sea aggregate leakages from innumerable distant fields, factories and households, so polluters do not pay for using it as a sink. No {{ref:nature-econ-621}} cover the oceans beyond national jurisdiction, so no one has an incentive to protect them from contamination or from taking too many fish. {{ref:nature-econ-633}} are non-rivalrous and non-excludable, a mirror image of {{ref:nature-econ-615}}. They are underproduced for the same reason that {{ref:nature-econ-615}} are overused.

nature-found-107.title: Soundscape ecology: listening to ecosystems
nature-found-107.text: The study of soundscapes covers the acoustic relationships between living organisms, human and other, and their environment. Soundscapes combine biophony from organisms, geophony from natural non-biological sources and anthropophony from humans. Anthropogenic noise, the subject of {{ref:nature-found-067}}, masks acoustic signals, harming communication, foraging and predator recognition across fish, amphibians, birds and mammals. Great tits in noisy urban territories sing at higher frequencies and with shorter, faster-repeated songs. Noise can reduce insect diversity and abundance, with possible knock-on effects on ecosystem services such as pollination. Natural soundscapes are now a conservation goal and may be considered ecosystem services provided by intact ecosystems.

nature-hist-027.title: The economics of biodiversity: how life props up the economy
nature-hist-027.text: The WWF's 2018 Living Planet Report argued that the whole global economy, worth US$125 trillion, ultimately relies on nature. The economics of biodiversity studies that dependence, and the harm economic activity does in return. Biodiversity underpins ecosystem services and affects how productive ecosystems are. It supplies food, medicines and industrial materials such as wood, cotton, wool and silk, and it supports recreation and tourism. It inspires design too. Copying natural models is another route, as when the ridges on humpback whale fins inspired wind turbine blades. Yet most species have never been assessed for their present or future economic importance. Economists still debate whether biodiversity should be valued mainly for its benefits to people, and what its value in itself might be.

nature-mkt-154.title: Divestment and the fossil fuel campaign
nature-mkt-154.text: Divestment is the reduction of an asset, or the sale of a business, for financial, ethical or political objectives. Firms divest to focus on core operations, raise cash, stabilise results, drop failing units, or comply with regulators. Shareholder pressure for social reasons is often called disinvestment, and has targeted apartheid South Africa, tobacco, factory farming and fossil fuels, the last coordinated by 350.org since the 2010s. As of July 2023, more than 1593 institutions holding over $40.5 trillion had begun or committed to selling off some holdings in fossil fuel companies. Financial research suggests it has raised investors' returns in the longer term.

nature-nbs-246.title: Agroecology: ecology applied to the farm
nature-nbs-246.text: Organics is practiced in 188 countries, and it is one of three certified forms of agroecology. Agroecology is the study and practice of applying ecological processes to farming, looking at links between plants, animals, people and the environment. The term can mean a science, a set of practices, or a social movement. It draws on agronomy, ecology, sociology, economics and history. It studies farm ecosystems' productivity, stability, sustainability and fairness, at scales from a gene to the globe. Unlike in natural ecology, human activity and economics are the main forces at work. Biodynamic farming, organics and China's Green Food are its certified varieties. Movements such as La Via Campesina use it to pursue {{ref:nature-nbs-317}}. Researchers heatedly debate which model of farming policy should support.

nature-nbs-317.title: Food sovereignty: who controls the food system
nature-nbs-317.text: Having enough food and controlling how it is grown are different questions. Food security is about access to enough food. Food sovereignty is the idea that people should control their own food systems, including how food is produced, distributed and consumed. Via Campesina coined the term in 1996. The 2007 Declaration of Nyeleni, from delegates of 80+ countries, defines it as peoples' right to healthy, culturally appropriate, ecologically sound food. As of 2020 at least seven countries had written it into their constitutions and laws. The idea is argued over. Advocates say the Green Revolution raised output without solving hunger because it ignored access to land and economic power. Critics say the movement rests on wrong assumptions about subsistence farming. A related right is seed sovereignty, to breed and exchange open-sourced seeds, argued for on biodiversity and grounds of coping with a changing climate as well as food justice.

nature-nbs-325.title: Detention basins: storing a storm and releasing it slowly
nature-nbs-325.text: A detention basin is an excavated area on or near a waterway that protects against flooding, and sometimes downstream erosion, by temporarily storing water. It lets large flows in and limits outflow through a small low opening sized to downstream culvert capacity, and it can control events such as a 1-in-100-year storm. Basins are usually built with new developments to handle runoff from impervious surfaces like roads, parking lots and rooftops. A basin with no permanent pool is a dry pond. One designed to hold some water permanently is a {{ref:nature-nbs-172}}, which manages quantity but has limited effect on water quality. Real-time control of outflow makes basins significantly better at retaining suspended solids and associated contaminants. Extended detention dry basins lengthen storage time beyond the 6 to 12 hours of basic ponds, allowing more settling of solids and cleaner water. Urban parks can serve as dual-purpose basins, acting as sports fields or parkland normally and storing stormwater in big storms; Joynton Park in Sydney is an example.

nature-nbs-333.title: How levees change rivers, floodplains and habitat
nature-nbs-333.text: A levee protects the land behind it, but it also cuts the river off from that land. Levees constrain flood pulses and the deposition of nutrients, organic material and sediment on floodplains and wetlands. Less overbank deposition can bring the wearing away of the coast and land loss downstream. The reverse is also seen: where levees were removed, riparian habitat and biodiversity increased.

nature-nbs-334.title: Phytoremediation: plants that clean contaminated ground
nature-nbs-334.text: Tobacco plants given bacterial nitroreductase genes removed TNT faster. That is phytoremediation: the use of living plants to clean up soil, air and water contaminated with pollutants. Its main mechanisms are {{ref:nature-nbs-335}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-336}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-338}} and phytofiltration. It is proposed as a sustainable alternative to conventional remediation, though it has never been used at large scales. Microbial bioremediation has so far been more successful. Breeding and genetic engineering can strengthen or add the abilities involved. Plant growth-promoting bacteria in the rhizosphere, the soil zone around roots, improve the results by raising biomass and by making heavy metals more mobile.

nature-nbs-344.title: Tillage classes by residue left on the surface
nature-nbs-344.text: One way to sort tillage is by what it leaves behind. Intensive tillage leaves under 15% residue cover on the soil surface. Reduced tillage leaves 15 to 30%, and {{ref:nature-nbs-291}} at least 30% during the critical erosion period. That cover slows water movement and erosion. It also benefits predatory arthropods and saves fuel, labour and soil compaction.

nature-pol-053.title: Cleaning up brownfields
nature-pol-053.text: Poisoned ground can be healed, though rarely by one method alone. Brownfield remediation is cleaning contaminated former industrial land so it can be reused. Techniques include heating soil in place, bioremediation, which uses living organisms to break pollutants down, oxidizing contaminants in place, and soil vapor extraction, which draws out polluting gases. They are often combined. Binders can be mixed into soil to stop chemicals leaching out. In {{ref:nature-nbs-334}}, deep-rooted plants draw heavy metals out of the soil.

nature-pol-067.title: Waste-to-energy: power from rubbish
nature-pol-067.text: Rubbish can keep the lights on. Waste-to-energy is generating power from municipal waste, by burning it, by capturing landfill gas, or through pyrolysis or gasification, which break waste down with heat. Older incinerators emitted many pollutants. New rules and technology changed that. US rules in 1995 and 2000 cut dioxin emissions from such plants by over 99% below 1990 levels, and mercury by over 90%. Because waste contains food, wood and paper, burning it can partly count as {{ref:nature-res-258}}, energy made from living material.

nature-pol-103.title: Putting a carbon price on shipping
nature-pol-103.text: Ships carry 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Charging for emissions in shipping means charging ships for the gases they emit. The price is meant to close the cost gap between heavy fuel oil and low-carbon fuels. That could break a stand-off in which fuel suppliers and shipowners each wait for the other. In 2023 the EU extended its carbon market ({{ref:nature-pol-253}}) to shipping, and the International Maritime Organization set a goal of net-zero shipping emissions by around 2050. An IMO scheme would be the first global system of its kind, but China, Brazil, South Africa and others oppose it as unfair to developing countries. Stakeholders also disagree over whether the revenue should stay in shipping or fund climate action generally.

nature-pol-112.title: Eco-tariffs: taxing trade to cut pollution
nature-pol-112.text: Should a country tax imports made with dirty processes? An eco-tariff, or environmental tariff, is a trade barrier such as an import or export tax used to reduce pollution. It targets goods with a large carbon footprint, or goods from countries with lax environmental rules; a {{ref:nature-pol-265}} is one type. Supporters say it could stop foreign countries gaining an advantage from weak rules and bring partners' standards into line. Critics argue it reduces trade without reaching the main sources of pollution, much of which arises within a country's own borders. Developing countries fear that environmental goals will be used as cover for shielding domestic industry from foreign competition. Import tariffs alone can also weaken export competitiveness and contribute to deindustrialization. Underneath lies an open question: does freer trade increase pollution, or, by raising incomes, end up reducing it?

nature-pol-113.title: Effluent: the wastewater that reaches rivers
nature-pol-113.text: Effluent is wastewater from sewers or industrial outlets that flows into rivers, lakes or the sea, treated or untreated. It can carry fats and oils, solvents, detergents, heavy metals and food waste from many industries. Even clean-looking water can harm. Warm cooling water from power stations causes {{ref:nature-res-262}}. In the United States, the Clean Water Act requires a permit for every direct discharge of effluent into surface waters.

nature-pol-155.title: The Clean Water Act: permits for every pipe
nature-pol-155.text: In the United States, a factory may not pour waste into a river without a permit. That rule comes from the Clean Water Act, the main federal law controlling pollution of surface waters, adopted in 1972 as amendments to the federal law on {{ref:nature-res-263}}. It created the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System, under which point sources such as factories and sewage plants need permits to discharge. Farm runoff and irrigation return flows were exempted as nonpoint sources. The 1972 Act also paid for municipal sewage plants, with federal grants covering 75% of project costs. Results are mixed. Its 1983 'fishable and swimmable' goal has not been met. More than half of stream and river miles, and about 70 percent of lakes, still violate water quality standards. Analysts credit it with controlling point sources but not nonpoint ones, and studies disagree on whether its benefits justify its costs.

nature-pol-159.title: The Endangered Species Act of 1973
nature-pol-159.text: On December 28, 1973, the United States signed one of its most powerful, and most controversial, environmental laws. The Endangered Species Act set out to stop extinctions caused by economic growth that ignored conservation. Its two aims are to prevent extinction and to recover species until they no longer need the law's protection. Agencies list species as 'endangered' or the lesser 'threatened'. Section 9 then bans 'take', meaning to harass, harm or hunt them. Since 1982, listing decisions must rest solely on biological and trade information, without weighing economic effects. Because habitat loss is the main threat to most imperiled species, agencies can designate {{ref:nature-pol-310}} zones. By August 2023, 1,780 species had been listed. Of those, 99% were still alive, but only 64 had recovered enough to leave the list. The American alligator, listed in 1967, was delisted as fully recovered twenty years later. The Act also underpins US {{ref:nature-mkt-127}}. Its economic costs keep it in dispute.

nature-pol-232.title: Pollution registers: the public's right to know
nature-pol-232.text: After the 1984 Bhopal disaster and the 1992 Rio conference, which affirmed people's right to be informed about toxic chemicals, several countries set up pollutant release and transfer registers. These systems collect and publish information on releases and transfers of hazardous substances from industrial and other facilities. The aim is to give nearby residents the same information as companies, since a level playing field matters for acceptance of permit decisions. A protocol to the {{ref:nature-gov-126}} requires its parties to set up such registers. That 2003 Kyiv Protocol was the first binding international instrument on them. The registers have a limit. Their data come mainly from facility questionnaires and remain the facilities' own estimates, even after official checks.

nature-pol-265.title: Carbon tariffs: pricing the carbon in imports
nature-pol-265.text: If one country prices carbon and its neighbor does not, factories may simply move. A carbon tariff, or border carbon adjustment, is a charge on imports according to the carbon emitted in making them ({{ref:nature-acct-061}}). Its usual aim is to prevent {{ref:nature-pol-252}}, the shift of emissions to states that have no carbon price. Likely targets include electricity from coal-fired power stations, iron and steel from blast furnaces, and fertilizer from the Haber process. California has applied one to imported electricity since 2011, and the EU and UK apply them from 2026 and 2027. Border adjustment is considered an economically efficient fix for leakage, but it might disguise trade barriers meant to shield home industry. Current WTO rules may prohibit some types, and the WTO has reached no conclusion.

nature-pol-290.title: How climate change denial works
nature-pol-290.text: Climate change denial is a form of science denial. It rejects, disputes or fights the extensive evidence for human-caused global warming and the scientific consensus on it. Those promoting it use rhetorical tactics to make a scientific controversy appear where none exists: raising unreasonable doubt about human causes and effects, and understating adaptation costs while overstating the costs of mitigation. Its tactics include delaying mitigation, pushing adaptation only, disputing IPCC processes, and promoting conspiracy theories. The downplaying approach was copied from tobacco lobbyists, who tried to prevent or delay regulation despite scientific evidence linking tobacco to lung cancer. ExxonMobil led climate change denial from the 1980s to the mid 2000s and helped prevent US ratification of the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}; research found its scientific opinion and public posture contradicted each other. A 2008 University of Central Florida study found that 92% of environmentally skeptical literature published in the US was partly or wholly affiliated with conservative think tanks. The campaigns have lowered public belief in climate change, which has affected legislative efforts to curb CO2 emissions. As of February 2024, at least 32 US lawsuits sought damages from the fossil fuel industry for spreading denial despite knowing the risks.

nature-pol-295.title: The incineration debate
nature-pol-295.text: Few waste plants divide a neighborhood like an incinerator. Using them for waste management weighs the economic appeal of local industry against health and environmental risk. Supporters say {{ref:nature-pol-294}} avoids landfill methane, saves landfill space where land is scarce, and replaces fossil power with partly biomass-based energy. They also note that in Europe the highest incineration rates generally go with top recycling performance. Critics say fly ash concentrates ecotoxic heavy metals and needs specialized landfills, and that the {{ref:nature-eecon-022}} prefers prevention, reuse and recycling. In the UK, the EU Landfill Directive led to the {{ref:nature-pol-117}} and the Landfill Allowance Trading Scheme. Business, regulators, activists and residents contest it over health, recycling and lock-in.

nature-pol-296.title: Black carbon: the soot that warms and kills
nature-pol-296.text: Black carbon is the light-absorbing form of elemental carbon left by heating material without oxygen or produced by incomplete combustion, as in soot. It forms from incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, biofuel and biomass and is fine {{ref:nature-pol-068}} that causes premature death and disability. About 20% of emissions come from biofuels, 40% from fossil fuels and 40% from open biomass burning. Developed countries were once the main source, but control technologies since the 1950s shifted most emissions to developing countries. Estimates say 640,000 to 4,900,000 premature deaths a year could be prevented with available mitigation measures. In soils black carbon is typically 1 to 6% of organic carbon, and Terra preta soils hold about three times the organic matter of surrounding soils.

nature-pol-297.title: Black carbon and the climate
nature-pol-297.text: Black carbon warms the climate by absorbing sunlight, altering clouds and darkening snow and ice. The IPCC's 2007 report put direct forcing from fossil-fuel black carbon at +0.2 W/m2 and the snow and ice {{ref:nature-nbs-090}} effect at an additional +0.1 W/m2. Later estimates rank it second after carbon dioxide. Estimates of direct forcing range from the IPCC's +0.34 W/m2 (plus or minus 0.25) to 0.9 W/m2 by Ramanathan and Carmichael. Because it stays in the air only weeks, cutting emissions may be the fastest way to slow near-term warming. A 2013 study found gas flares contributed over 40% of black carbon deposited in the Arctic.

nature-pol-299.title: Environmental remediation: cleaning up contaminated land
nature-pol-299.text: Before a polluted site can be reused, someone has to clean it. Environmental remediation is the removal, treatment or containment of hazardous substances in soil, groundwater and sediment. Assessment begins when a site is suspected contaminated, often with a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment guided by the site's history. Waste can be removed and transported off-site for disposal, or contained by physical barriers such as slurry walls. Regulations may require remediation before land is redeveloped, and voluntary cleanups can earn incentives, such as New York State's Brownfield Cleanup Program. Cleanup standards differ: the US uses EPA Regional Screening Levels, Europe has the Dutch standards, and Canadian provinces set their own. In the US a tax on polluting industries funds {{ref:nature-pol-176}} cleanups of abandoned sites. Elsewhere sites are often rezoned to higher uses so land value covers cleanup costs. Remediation can face local resistance to rezoning; main impacts are noise, dust, odour and some added health risk.

nature-pol-303.title: Biofuel: fuel grown in a season
nature-pol-303.text: Biofuel is made over a short time span from biomass, rather than by the very slow natural processes that form fossil fuels. It can come from plants or from agricultural, domestic or industrial bio waste, and is mostly used for transport but also for heating and electricity. It is regarded as a renewable energy source, yet it faces criticism over the food-versus-fuel debate, varied sustainability assessments, and {{ref:nature-eco-053}} and {{ref:nature-eco-035}} from production. Global production was 81 Mtoe in 2017, about 3% a year above 2010. The US led with 37 Mtoe, then Brazil and South America at 23 Mtoe and Europe at 12 Mtoe. Emissions are not inherently carbon-neutral: they depend on feedstock, processing, transport and land-use change, and range from -127.1 gCO2eq per MJ with carbon capture to above 95 gCO2eq per MJ where land-use change is large. EU and UK policies require biofuels to deliver at least 65% greenhouse gas savings against fossil fuels (70% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin). The International Resource Panel concluded that biofuels differ in their effects on climate, the security of energy supply and ecosystems, so effects should be assessed over the whole life cycle.

nature-pol-309.title: Indirect land use change: the emissions biofuels cause elsewhere
nature-pol-309.text: A biofuel can look clean at the field and dirty on the far side of the world. The indirect form of {{ref:nature-res-108}} is the unintended extra carbon emissions from cropland expanding elsewhere to meet global demand for {{ref:nature-pol-303}}. Farmers worldwide respond to higher crop prices by clearing pristine land to replace the food crops diverted to biofuel. Because rainforests and {{ref:nature-eco-467}} store carbon, clearing them raises net greenhouse gas emissions. Some authors argue it also affects biodiversity, water quality, food prices and supply, land tenure, worker migration and community stability. Before 2008, life-cycle studies found corn, cellulosic and Brazilian sugarcane ethanol cut emissions versus gasoline, but none counted these effects. A 2008 Searchinger paper concluded that indirect effects offset the direct gains of corn and cellulosic ethanol. Payback was 4 years for Brazilian sugarcane, 167 for US corn and 52 for cellulosic ethanol, over a 30-year horizon. Critics such as Wang and Haq called the assumptions outdated, and Searchinger replied that ignoring these emissions is wrong however hard they are to predict. The size of the emissions was disputed by the studies' authors and critics. In 2009 the California Air Resources Board included these indirect effects in California's {{ref:nature-pol-165}}, in force in 2011. A 2010 Brazil study projected indirect deforestation of 121,970 km2 by 2020 from sugarcane ethanol and soybean biodiesel, a carbon debt taking about 250 years to repay.

nature-pol-314.title: Perverse incentives and the cobra effect
nature-pol-314.text: In Hanoi in 1902, a bounty paid 1 cent per rat tail. Rat catchers cut off the tails and released the rats to breed more. A perverse incentive is a structure that produces undesirable results, especially effects unexpected and contrary to what its designers intended. Horst Siebert coined the name "cobra effect" in 2001 from a British Raj anecdote about a bounty on dead cobras. That anecdote is disputed: a 2025 investigation found no contemporary records of cobra breeding in British India, said the Madras bounty was scaled back over cost, not fraud, and urged retiring the term. Other cases hold up better. At Fort Benning a $40 bounty per feral pig tail coincided with a rising pig population; feed bait raised fertility and survival, and hunters preferred large males over females and juveniles. Endangered Species Act restrictions on landowners can encourage preemptive habitat destruction. A {{ref:nature-mkt-081}} scheme gave one of the highest bounties for destroying the refrigerant byproduct HFC-23, so firms made more refrigerant to earn credits; the EU suspended such credits in 2013. Grandfathered emission permits, offsets, {{ref:nature-mkt-104}} credits and subsidised insurance against flood damage have all drawn the same criticism.

nature-res-229.title: Dutch disease: when a boom hollows out the rest
nature-res-229.text: In 1959 the Netherlands discovered the Groningen gas field, and Dutch manufacturing then declined. In 1977 The Economist coined a name for the pattern: Dutch disease. It describes the apparent link between a boom in one sector, such as natural resources, and a decline in others such as manufacturing or agriculture. The mechanism runs through the currency. Boom revenues strengthen it, making the country's other exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper, so those sectors lose ground. Any large inflow of foreign currency can do this, including foreign aid and foreign direct investment. Trade theory says resource-rich countries should specialize in extraction, but this backfires when the resource runs down, because manufacturing cannot return as fast as it left. Diagnosis is hard. Still, very large, unexpected oil and gas discoveries do on average seem to raise the currency's price-adjusted value against others and shrink lagging sectors. Remedies include saving boom revenue abroad in a {{ref:nature-res-243}}, running budget surpluses, and investing in education and infrastructure for the lagging sectors.

nature-res-256.title: The EU Common Fisheries Policy
nature-res-256.text: The Common Fisheries Policy is the European Union's fisheries policy: it sets catch quotas, gives member states access to one another's exclusive economic zones and manages sustainable fishing in the EU's zone. Member states may implement its principles through licences, limited entry or {{ref:nature-res-018}}, and regulations cover gear and closed areas. Enforcement is left to member states, with a community inspection service checking them. The 2013 reform, in force from 1 January 2014, was meant to protect endangered stocks and end discards, with maximum sustainable yield to apply from 2015. Critics say per-species quotas force fish to be thrown overboard dead, and that its centralised top-down approach should give way to participatory governance. Commentators disagree on whether the policy harmed stocks or merely failed to reverse a decline that predated it. A 2010 study traced stock depletion to mismanagement long before the policy, with British catch rates down 94% over 118 years.

nature-res-257.title: Agriculture: feeding cities, reshaping the land
nature-res-257.text: Farming covers 4.8 billion ha, about one-third of the Earth's land, and touches land and water more than any other economic sector. Agriculture is the cultivation of soil and the planting and harvesting of food and non-food crops, together with livestock production. Broader definitions also take in forestry and aquaculture, though horticulture and forestry are often left out in practice. Its surpluses let people live in cities and let population grow far beyond what hunting and gathering could sustain. The cost shows up in {{ref:nature-res-107}}. Expansion drives deforestation and degrades carbon-rich ecosystems such as peatlands, and about 40% of agricultural land is seriously degraded. Livestock occupy 70% of that land, which is 30% of the planet's land surface. Farming pushed for maximum output per hectare raised yields by substituting synthetic fertilizers and pesticides for labour, but it increased water pollution and often relied on subsidies. Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute between 13% and 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions, so it is tied to {{ref:nature-hist-007}}. FAO estimates that farms must produce about 50% more food, feed and fibre by 2050 than in 2012, adding pressure on water, land and soil.

nature-res-263.title: Controlling water pollution at the source
nature-res-263.text: Municipal wastewater can be treated in centralized plants, decentralized systems, {{ref:nature-nbs-220}} or septic tanks; waste stabilization ponds are a low-cost option. Treated industrial effluent may be reused or released to a sanitary sewer or surface water. Construction sediment is managed with erosion controls such as mulching and sediment controls such as basins and silt fences. Controlling urban runoff means slowing stormwater flow and cutting pollutant discharges. In the United States the 1972 Clean Water Act amendments set up the main framework for improving water quality in surface waters.

nature-val-008.title: Cost-effectiveness analysis: the cheapest way to a goal
nature-val-008.text: Sometimes the goal is fixed and the only question is how to reach it cheaply. Cost-effectiveness analysis compares the costs and outcomes of different courses of action without putting a money value on the outcomes. Unlike {{ref:nature-val-001}}, it does not monetise the effect, which makes it common in health care, where pricing health is seen as inappropriate. Results are usually a ratio of cost to a health gain such as years of life; the most common outcome measure is the {{ref:nature-val-026}}. A 1995 review of over 500 life-saving interventions found a median of $42,000 per life-year saved. It also suits some environmental goals. For a single physical outcome, such as cutting energy use, it can replace cost-benefit analysis and is less laborious. It is preferred in climate economics when the benefits of mitigation and adaptation are hard to express in money. Distributional cost-effectiveness analysis extends it to weigh how outcomes are spread, trading equity against efficiency. Policy goals are often set politically, such as the Clean Air Act acid rain cut of 10 million tons of sulfur dioxide below 1980 levels, without knowing whether the target is efficient. A policy can still be judged cost-effective. Pollution reduction is split cost-effectively across sources only when all face the same marginal abatement cost. Otherwise, shifting cleanup from a high-cost to a low-cost source cuts total cost.

nature-val-106.title: Pitfalls in cost estimation
nature-val-106.text: A careless cost estimate can make a good policy look bad, or the reverse. Careful estimates must avoid four common mistakes: ignoring opportunity costs, using the wrong counterfactual, counting costs that would have occurred anyway and ignoring market changes. Opportunity costs are not on accounting sheets and are often overlooked. Studies of US endangered-species recovery spending used only direct government costs because opportunity costs are hard to measure. A cursory before-and-after comparison wrongly credits a policy with all cost changes. After the Deepwater Horizon drilling restrictions oil prices rose, but part of the rise came from recovering demand, so the true counterfactual is the price without the restrictions. Only costs caused by the policy count. Temporary stormwater controls already required during construction should not be charged to a new rule requiring no stormwater runoff after building. {{ref:nature-mkt-144}} is contested in benefit estimation too: some lands paid not to be deforested might not have been, or landowners may be paid by several sources for the same activity. Markets also move. A methyl bromide ban would raise strawberry production costs, lowering sales. The social cost is the deadweight loss on unsold strawberries plus higher costs on those still sold, which is below the simple estimate that costs all pre-ban output.

nature-val-107.title: Regulation: rules that steer markets
nature-val-107.text: Every speed limit and every pollution cap is regulation. It is the management of complex systems according to a set of rules and trends. State-mandated regulation is government intervention in the private market to produce outcomes that would not otherwise occur, from consumer protection to technological advancement. It may prescribe or proscribe conduct (command-and-control), calibrate incentives, or shape preferences. Common examples include limits on environmental pollution, minimum wages, labelling rules and {{ref:nature-pol-177}}. A critical question is whether the regulator has enough information to make ex-ante regulation more efficient than ex-post liability for harm, or whether self-regulation is preferable. Modern industrial regulation traces to the UK Railway Regulation Act 1844. In the 1960s and 1970s US concern over {{ref:nature-pol-040}} led to detailed laws creating the EPA and OSHA.

nature-val-112.title: Ecological modernization: can markets and states fix the environment?
nature-val-112.text: Can the economy be greened without being slowed? Ecological modernization is a school of thought arguing that the state and the market can work together to protect the environment. It emerged in the early 1980s among scholars at Free University and the Social Science Research Centre in Berlin, including Joseph Huber, Martin Jänicke and Udo Simonis. Its basic assumption is that economy and ecology can be combined: productive use of natural resources and environmental media can be a source of growth, like labour and capital productivity. Its tools include energy efficiency and {{ref:nature-eecon-191}}, clean technologies, environmental management, substitution of hazardous substances and product design for environment, with radical innovations changing industrial metabolism. It also draws on {{ref:nature-eecon-017}}, {{ref:nature-acct-050}} of products, and 'cradle to cradle' manufacturing as against 'cradle to grave'. Scholars differ on whether it is only techno-industrial policy or includes cultural change, and on whether government, markets or civil society should lead. All expect innovative structural change. Business may favour it because it meets the {{ref:nature-acct-114}} without challenging free-market principles. Many views within the environmental movement see free trade and self-regulation as part of the problem. Critics call it {{ref:nature-nbs-075}} that leaves capitalism's impulses to degrade the environment intact. They say it ignores environmental racism, applies mostly to Germany and the Netherlands, and rests on an impossible 'sustainable growth'. Its effectiveness and applicability remain a contentious area of environmental social science.

nature-val-114.title: The normal distribution and its bell curve
nature-val-114.text: Most of the statistics behind valuation rest on one shape. The normal distribution is the bell-shaped probability distribution defined by a mean, which sets its location, and a variance, which sets its squared scale. It is symmetric around its mean, which is also its mode and median. About 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two and about 99.7% within three: the 68-95-99.7 or 3-sigma rule. The standard normal is the case with mean 0 and variance 1; any normal variable can be built by scaling it by the standard deviation and shifting it by the mean. Its density is written with the Greek letter phi and its cumulative distribution function with capital Phi. The quantile function of the standard normal is the probit function. Among all distributions with a given mean and variance, it has the maximum {{ref:nature-eecon-109}}. It is the only one whose cumulants beyond the mean and variance are zero. Any linear combination of independent normal variables is itself normal, and the sum of squares of independent standard normals has a chi-squared distribution. Occurrences are loosely exact, approximate or merely assumed, and Ioannidis warns that using normal standard deviations to validate findings leaves non-normal phenomena untested.
